newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's cherished Vespa has 50th birthday revamp.
newsitem.headline: Italy's cherished Vespa has 50th birthday revamp.

text.p: The Vespa, the much-loved motor scooter that did for transport in post-war Italy what the Model-T Ford car did for the United States, celebrated its 50th birthday in style on Friday with a hip new look.
Piaggio, the family-owned firm that has been turning out Vespas since 1946, launched two new models of the cult classic complete with new environmental features for the 21st century.
"The Vespa was the Italian product that introduced Italy to the world," said chairman Giovanni Alberto Agnelli.

"The challenge we face is to reinterpret not just the legend but also the function of the Vespa in today's post-industrial society," he told an anniversary news conference attended by more than 500 journalists from around the world.
Traditionalists need not fear. The Vespa has not lost an ounce of the "dolce vita" appeal glamorised by Audrey Hepburn and Gregory Peck in the 1952 movie "Roman Holiday".
If anything, the retro-style has been given a boost with sleeker styling and a new range of colours -- including pastel tones and the olive green of the original Vespas.

Contours on the new 50cc Vespa ET2 and 125cc Vespa ET4 are rounder, the saddle is bigger and more comfortable and some original features, including slanted letters spelling out Vespa -- "wasp" in Italian -- on the front, have been reintroduced.
The structure is still made of steel, not plastic.
But the 50cc model boasts the world's first fuel-injection two-stroke engine, making it the only scooter to meet European Union rules on exhaust and noise emissions for the year 2000.
The 125cc version has a new "clean" four-stroke engine. Both models purr rather than buzz and are automatic, ridding the rider of the hassle of kick-starting or changing gears.

The new-generation Vespas run on lead-free petrol, rather than a mixture of petrol and oil, meaning the company can now target North American markets where its old scooters failed to meet rules on emissions.

Piaggio, which leads the European scooter sector and is fourth worldwide behind Japanese giants Honda, Suzuki and Yamaha, says it cost 35 billion lire ($21 million) and took three years to develop the new Vespas in an ever tougher market.

"We're behind some of our objectives because the market has contracted a bit but turnover is higher than last year," said spokesman Enea Nepentini. The company is related to Italy's carmaker Fiat, controlled by the Agnelli family.
The original Vespa was the brainchild of Enrico Piaggio, the son of an entrepreneur whose aviation factory was bombed out of business at the end of World War Two.

"I want a vehicle that puts Italy on two wheels, but I don't want the usual motorbike," said Piaggio, who saw the scooter -- which had been around since the 1920s without success -- as a potentially mass-market product to get the factory going again.
The first Vespa, designed by engineer Corradino D'Ascanio who invented the world's first fully-functional helicopter, was launched in April 1946. Its shape earned it the famous name.
"It looks just like a wasp!" history records Piaggio as exclaiming when he saw the buzzing contraption with its "head", narrow waist and flared back tapering to a point.

The Vespa soon became an affordable, sturdy means of transport for whole families, giving young people their first taste of independent travel. Enthusiasts caught the bug. One, Giorgio Bettinelli, has been right around the world on a Vespa and there are clubs in 23 countries from Japan to Finland.
The new-look Vespas broadly got the thumbs-up from motoring journalists and aficionados attending the launch.
Even Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who is better known for riding a bicyle, said he was a fan. "It's a nice mix of harking back to old times and novelty," he said. ($1=1524)
